details:
**Ulysses and Leopold Bloom**
Joyce's 1922 modernist masterpiece, which follows the Jewish advertising canvasser Leopold Bloom as he wanders Dublin on a single day, June 16, 1904 (now celebrated as "Bloomsday"). Its 18 episodes, grouped into three parts, parallel Homer's Odyssey, and it makes heavy use of stream of consciousness.

**Molly Bloom's soliloquy, "yes I said yes I will Yes"**
The final episode of Ulysses, "Penelope," is a nearly unpunctuated stream-of-consciousness monologue by Bloom's wife Molly. In bed, she muses about her affair that afternoon with Hugh "Blazes" Boylan and remembers accepting Leopold's proposal, ending with "yes I said yes I will Yes."

**"The Dead" and Gabriel Conroy**
The final and longest story in Dubliners. At a party, the tenor Bartell D'Arcy sings "The Lass of Aughrim," which reminds Gabriel Conroy's wife Gretta of Michael Furey, a boy who loved her and died young ("I think he died for me"). Gabriel has an epiphany as he watches the snow "faintly falling... upon all the living and the dead," including Furey's grave.

**The Morkan sisters' party**
The setting of "The Dead": the annual Christmas-season dance held by Gabriel's aunts Kate and Julia Morkan and their niece Mary Jane. There, the nationalist Molly Ivors teases Gabriel as a "West Briton" for writing reviews for a pro-British newspaper, and Gabriel worries whether to quote Robert Browning in his after-dinner speech.

**Stephen Dedalus and Buck Mulligan**
Joyce's alter ego, the hero of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man and a central figure in Ulysses. Ulysses opens with "Stately, plump Buck Mulligan" shaving atop the Martello tower where Stephen lives. In "Nestor," Stephen teaches a history class on Pyrrhus attended by the ugly student Cyril Sargent. He tells Mr. Deasy that God is "a shout in the street" and that "history is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake."

**Other episodes of Ulysses: "Ithaca," "Circe," "Nausicaa"**
"Ithaca" is written as a question-and-answer catechism describing Bloom and Stephen's return to Bloom's home at 7 Eccles Street. "Circe" is written as a play set in Dublin's red-light district: Bloom hallucinates turning into a woman dominated by "Bello" (the brothel-keeper Bella Cohen), rescues Stephen, and sees the ghost of his dead son Rudy. In the controversial "Nausicaa," Bloom watches Gerty MacDowell on the beach. Another episode is "Lotus-Eaters."

**Father Arnall's hell sermon**
In A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Stephen goes on a religious retreat where Father Arnall preaches terrifying sermons on death, judgment, and the torments of Hell. Overcome with guilt over his visits to prostitutes, Stephen confesses and briefly becomes fervently devout, before ultimately rejecting the Church to become an artist.

**"Araby"**
A Dubliners story in which a boy on North Richmond Street becomes infatuated with Mangan's sister and promises to bring her a gift from the Araby bazaar. His uncle comes home late and gives him a florin, and he arrives as the bazaar is closing. He sees himself as "a creature driven and derided by vanity," and his eyes burn "with anguish and anger."

**Opening and childhood of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man**
Joyce's 1916 semi-autobiographical novel opens with a baby-talk story: "Once upon a time... there was a moocow coming down along the road and this moocow... met a nicens little boy named baby tuckoo." At Clongowes Wood College, the bully Wells shoulders Stephen into a cesspool (the "square ditch"). At Christmas dinner, Dante Riordan and Mr. Casey argue bitterly over the fall of Charles Stewart Parnell.

**Stephen Hero, the villanelle, and Emma**
Stephen Hero was Joyce's earlier draft of Portrait, published posthumously. In Portrait, Stephen writes a villanelle for his beloved Emma that repeats "Are you not weary of ardent ways?" Earlier, rumors spread that some Clongowes boys ran away because they stole altar wine from the sacristy or were caught "smugging."

**Finnegans Wake and "riverrun"**
Joyce's final, dreamlike novel (1939), written in a punning language drawing on dozens of languages. It begins mid-sentence with "riverrun, past Eve and Adam's... by a commodius vicus of recirculation back to Howth Castle and Environs." The book's unfinished last sentence loops back to this opening.

**HCE, ALP, and "Three quarks for Muster Mark"**
Finnegans Wake centers on the Dublin publican H. C. Earwicker (Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker, whose initials recur as "Here Comes Everybody" and "Howth Castle and Environs") and his wife Anna Livia Plurabelle (ALP), who is also the River Liffey. The line "Three quarks for Muster Mark" gave physicist Murray Gell-Mann the name "quark."

**"A Painful Case" and "Ivy Day in the Committee Room"**
In "A Painful Case," the solitary James Duffy breaks off a friendship with Mrs. Emily Sinico and later reads in the newspaper that she has died. In "Ivy Day in the Committee Room," canvassers for the mayoral candidate Richard Tierney gather on the anniversary of Parnell's death, and Joe Hynes is accused of spying for Colgan.

**Other stories in Dubliners**
The 15-story collection (1914) opens with "The Sisters," in which a boy deals with the death of the priest Father Flynn. In "An Encounter," a strange old man says boys who talk to girls should be whipped. In "A Little Cloud," Little Chandler is shaken by his successful friend Ignatius Gallaher. In "Clay," the laundress Maria sings the same verse of "I Dreamt that I Dwelt" twice after a Halloween game. Other stories include "Eveline" and "After the Race," in which Jimmy Doyle tries to fit in with Charles Segouin and his friends.

**Chamber Music**
Joyce's first book, a 1907 collection of 36 love poems. One of his poems was included in Ezra Pound's anthology Des Imagistes.
